question: An analyst has a Research-mode output on competitor pricing, with citations against most claims, that will inform a pricing decision. Which two validation steps are most useful? Select two.
options: A) Confirm the headline figure against the company's own records rather than one source.
B) Run the same research request again and accept the result if the two broadly agree.
C) Open a sample of cited pages and confirm each says what the summary claims.
D) Use the number of citations shown as a rough measure of how reliable the output is.
E) Accept anything carrying a citation and spend the time only on uncited statements.
correct_answers: A) Confirm the headline figure against the company's own records rather than one source.
C) Open a sample of cited pages and confirm each says what the summary claims.
explanations: Correct. Bringing in an independent record is a different technique from checking sources: it avoids treating Claude as a singular source of truth on a decision that matters.
Two runs can be wrong in the same way, so agreement between them is a consistency signal rather than any evidence about accuracy.
Correct. A citation shows where a claim came from, not that it was read correctly. Opening the page is what catches a figure taken out of context or from the wrong year.
Citation count measures volume, not quality. A heavily cited output can rest on weak sources, and a lightly cited one can be entirely sound.
A citation is not a guarantee, and cited claims are precisely the ones that feel safe to skip, which is what lets a misread source pass through unchallenged.
